Hail
hale
n. (frozen rain falling in stones; a standing instrument of divine judgment; rendering Hebrew barad, Greek chalaza)
From the Saxon hagal. The English word is a homonym of the greeting hail (from Old Norse heill, health), which is unrelated; the weather word is a Germanic term for the ice that falls in stones.

Biblical Definition

Hail is the weapon Scripture reaches for when God fights from the sky. It is the seventh plague on Egypt: “the LORD sent thunder and hail, and the fire ran along upon the ground; and the LORD rained hail upon the land of Egypt” (Exodus 9:23) — and the account is careful to note that Goshen had none, so that the storm distinguished between peoples. It fights for Israel at Bethhoron: “the LORD cast down great stones from heaven upon them unto Azekah, and they died: they were more which died with hailstones than they whom the children of Israel slew with the sword” (Joshua 10:11). The tally is stated deliberately — God killed more of the enemy than the army did, on a day when Israel was doing everything right. Isaiah makes it the destroyer of false security: “the hail shall sweep away the refuge of lies, and the waters shall overflow the hiding place” (Isaiah 28:17), in a passage where the true foundation is the tried stone laid in Zion. And Revelation gives the last hailstorm: “there fell upon men a great hail out of heaven, every stone about the weight of a talent: and men blasphemed God because of the plague of the hail” (Revelation 16:21). Under a judgment that plain, men still cursed — which is Scripture's standing answer to the notion that sufficient evidence produces repentance.

Webster 1828 Definition

Frozen rain in stones, and Scripture's weapon from the sky. It falls on Egypt and spares Goshen, kills more at Bethhoron than the sword, sweeps away the refuge of lies — and in Revelation is cursed rather than heeded.

expand to see more

HAIL, n. [Sax. hagal.] Masses or particles of ice falling from the clouds, usually in showers, and generally in warm weather.

2. HAIL, v.i. To pour down particles of ice, or frozen vapors.

3. HAILSTONE, n. A single mass or particle of ice falling from a cloud.

4. In Scripture, an instrument of divine judgment; the hail shall sweep away the refuge of lies, Is. 28.

5. HAIL, exclam. [Sax. hal, whole, sound.] A term of salutation, expressive of a wish for health; a distinct word.

Key Scripture

Exodus 9:23 — "And Moses stretched forth his rod toward heaven: and the LORD sent thunder and hail, and the fire ran along upon the ground; and the LORD rained hail upon the land of Egypt."

Joshua 10:11 — "And it came to pass, as they fled from before Israel, and were in the going down to Bethhoron, that the LORD cast down great stones from heaven upon them unto Azekah, and they died: they were more which died with hailstones than they whom the children of Israel slew with the sword."

Isaiah 28:17 — "Judgment also will I lay to the line, and righteousness to the plummet: and the hail shall sweep away the refuge of lies, and the waters shall overflow the hiding place."

Revelation 16:21 — "And there fell upon men a great hail out of heaven, every stone about the weight of a talent: and men blasphemed God because of the plague of the hail; for the plague thereof was exceeding great."

Modern Corruption

Natural judgments are treated as purely meteorological, so that Scripture's claim that God governs storms is set aside — while Revelation 16 quietly refutes the belief that clearer evidence would produce faith.

expand to see more

The instinct of the age is that weather is weather and that any theological reading of it is superstition. Scripture's claim is not that every storm is a judgment, and Christian prudence should be slow to assign meaning to particular disasters — our Lord expressly refused that reasoning about the tower of Siloam (Luke 13:4). But Scripture does claim that God governs the weather absolutely and that he has used it in judgment by name and on the record. The plague on Egypt was announced in advance, spared Goshen precisely, and stopped when Moses spread his hands. That is not weather with a moral gloss added; it is a stated act with a stated purpose, and the alternative is to treat the narrative as fiction.

The principle to recover is Revelation 16:21, which is the most important verse in Scripture about the limits of evidence. Hailstones of a talent weight fall out of heaven, the plague is unmistakable, and the recorded human response is blasphemy. Men did not lack proof; they lacked a new heart. This is why the Reformed doctrine of total depravity is not pessimism about human behaviour but realism about the will: the natural man does not fail to believe because the case is thin, and no display of power has ever converted anyone. The Spirit gives sight, or the brightest evidence is only better-lit darkness.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew barad is hail, and abne barad, hailstones. Greek chalaza is hail, used in Revelation's trumpet and vial judgments.

expand to see more

Hebrew barad (H1259) — hail; the seventh plague and the stones of Bethhoron.

Hebrew eben (H68) — a stone; joined with barad for hailstones.

Hebrew machseh (H4268) — a refuge, shelter; the refuge of lies swept away in Isaiah 28:17.

Greek chalaza (G5464) — hail; the great hail of Revelation 16:21.

Greek talantiaios (G5006) — of a talent's weight; the measure of each falling stone.

Usage

"Of the plague on Egypt: the LORD rained hail upon the land of Egypt (Exodus 9:23)."

"Of God killing more than the army: they were more which died with hailstones (Joshua 10:11)."

"Of false security destroyed: the hail shall sweep away the refuge of lies (Isaiah 28:17)."
